The reproductive biology of Macropus antilopinus is characterized by a maximum annual output of one joey per female per year, with females capable of producing a single offspring per birth event [N_R_i = single offspring per birth event] and, under optimal conditions, raising one offspring annually [Ri = one offspring annually]. This modest reproductive rate, observed at the species' typical core body temperature of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C], reflects the energetic demands of rearing a single, relatively large offspring over an extended lactation period. At birth, the altricial neonate is remarkably diminutive; newborn joeys weigh just 0.703 grams [Wwb = 0.703 grams], a mass that represents a minute fraction of the mother's body weight. This tiny neonatal mammal must immediately crawl to the pouch, where it will undergo the majority of its early development while continuously suckling. Such an extreme altricial birth strategy is characteristic of macropodids and is thought to minimize the energetic burden on the gestating female during the brief period of intrauterine development.

The gestation period in Macropus antilopinus lasts for 34 days [tg = 34 days] when measured at the maternal core temperature of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C], a remarkably short duration for a mammal of its size. This abbreviated gestation is a hallmark of macropodid reproduction: the embryo undergoes a rapid developmental phase in utero before the tiny joey is born in an almost embryonic state. Following parturition, the neonate is entirely dependent on milk provided within the pouch. The suckling juvenile remains continuously attached to a teat for several weeks, during which time it grows substantially. The mother's lactation effort is considerable; the average daily milk production measured at 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C] is approximately 99726.03 joules per day , a value that sustains the offspring's rapid mass gain throughout the nursing stage. This substantial energetic transfer to a single offspring over an extended period constrains the potential for more frequent reproductive events.

Pouch exit and weaning represent critical transitional milestones in the life history of the antilopine wallaby. The time since birth at weaning is 426 days since birth [tx = 426 days since birth] at the typical maternal temperature of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C], marking the point at which the young animal achieves nutritional independence from its mother. By this stage, the weaned juvenile has reached a wet weight at weaning of 7500 grams [Wwx = 7500 grams], a roughly ten-thousand-fold increase over its birth mass that underscores the intensive maternal investment during the pre-weaning period. After weaning, the juvenile continues to grow and develop independently, refining its foraging skills and gradually increasing its body reserves. The transition to nutritional emancipation is not abrupt; young wallabies may continue to associate with their mother for some time after weaning, but they no longer rely on her milk for their daily metabolic requirements.

Sexual maturation in Macropus antilopinus is a relatively protracted process compared to the short gestation period. The time since birth at puberty is 639 days since birth [tp = 639 days since birth] when measured at 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C], a value that indicates individuals do not attain reproductive maturity until well into their second year of life. At the onset of puberty, females have typically reached a wet weight at puberty of 12500 grams [Wwp = 12500 grams], indicating that a substantial body mass threshold must be achieved before the reproductive axis becomes fully active. This delayed maturation, consistent with other large macropodids, is thought to be an adaptive response to the species' unpredictable savanna environment, where postponing reproduction until a robust body condition is attained may enhance the survival prospects of both the female and her subsequent offspring. The onset of gonadal activity marks the beginning of an individual's potential contribution to population recruitment, and females may enter oestrus shortly after attaining this developmental stage.

Adult body size and maximum longevity are two key parameters that frame the overall life-history strategy of Macropus antilopinus. The ultimate wet weight, representing the maximum body mass attained by fully grown adults, is 17500 grams [Wwi = 17500 grams], placing this wallaby among the larger members of its genus and reflecting the high-quality forage available in its tropical savanna habitat. This adult body mass is achieved after a prolonged period of growth following weaning and the attainment of sexual maturity. In terms of lifespan, the maximum longevity recorded for this species, assessed at a core body temperature of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C], is 10 years [am = 10 years], a moderate duration that aligns with the pace of life typical of medium-sized macropodids. This lifespan reflects a balance between the risks of predation and environmental stochasticity in the tropical savannas of northern Australia and the intrinsic physiological limits imposed by the species' developmental and reproductive schedule.
